So, Diego, let’s practice the first question. Tell me about yourself.
I’m a dermatology resident from Brazil. I graduated from medical school there, and since then I have focused on skin disease.
Good start. Why dermatology?
The turning point came in my first year, when we caught a melanoma very early. After that, I decided to pursue dermatology.
And what have you done to prepare for the United States?
I have read dermatology articles in English every week for years, and I have started my Step 3 preparation.
Have you ever worked in an American hospital?
Not yet. I haven’t done a rotation here, but I would like to shadow a dermatologist next year.
That’s honest, and it sounds good. Any setbacks?
My speaking was weak, so this year I started English classes twice a week. In hindsight, it was the best decision I made.

Every interview season I ask the same first question: tell me about yourself. And every season, many international applicants make the same mistake. They start at birth. I do not need to know where you went to high school. I need about ninety seconds, and I need a shape. Start with the present: who you are now and what you have been doing. Then go back to one turning point, one moment when your direction changed, and tell it with real details: when it happened, where you were, what you did. Then come back to now, and tell me where you want to go. The grammar does a lot of the work for you. When you say I have worked in dermatology for three years, you are talking about now. When you say in my second year I saw a patient who changed my mind, you are telling a story. Applicants who mix those two get lost, and so do I. One more thing: do not read me a list of your achievements. A setback that you learned from stands out more than ten prizes.

I graduated from medical school in Bogota in 2014, and I have lived in the United States for six years now. People ask me how I did it, and the honest answer is: slowly. My first application did not work. I applied to forty programs, and I did not get a single interview. That was the biggest setback of my life. In hindsight, it was also the turning point. I looked at my application again and I saw the problem: there was nothing American in it. So I spent a year shadowing a family doctor in Florida, and I wrote a new personal statement. The second time, I got eleven interviews, and I matched in internal medicine. Since then, I have finished my residency, I have passed Step 3, and I have started a fellowship. I have never forgotten that first year, though. When young doctors write to me, I tell them: your story does not need to be perfect. It needs to be true, and it needs to show what you have learned.
